newsitem.title: CHINA: Expectations grow for China credit easing in H2.
newsitem.headline: Expectations grow for China credit easing in H2.

text.p: Expectations are growing that China will ease credit in the second half of this year but central bank worries over the soaring stock market could delay the move, analysts and bankers said on Friday.

Cash-starved state firms are crying out for funds and this week's release of low inflation data has revived speculation of a credit easing through either a cut in the bank reserve ratio or a reduction in bank interest rates.
China's retail price inflation rose 0.8 percent in May compared with the same month in 1996, while consumer price inflation was up 2.8 percent year-on-year, the State Statistical Bureau said.
"It's already time for the central bank to cut interest rates further, but I think their concern is the stock market," said Jason Kwok, chief economist for Citibank NA in Hong Kong.
"One thing the government doesn't want to do is cut interest rates and fuel speculation in the stock market," he said.
Securities authorities since May have stepped up a campaign to curb speculation in the stock market, recently removing the heads of two banks and three securities firms for trading irregularities.

The timing of a credit easing would depend on the judgement of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, that such a move could be made safely without causing money to pour back into the stock market, analysts said.
The central bank is considering bond issues or limits on refinancing for banks along with any credit easing in a bid to control the overall liquidity in the system, bankers said.
An initial credit easing would most likely take the form of a cut in the bank reserve ratio, the sum banks are required to deposit with the central bank as a proportion of total deposits, they said.
China's bank reserve ratio currently stands at 13 percent and the market has for several months expected a three percentage point cut to 10 percent.
"Everyone agrees there will be a cut in the bank reserve ratio this year, but no one knows exactly when," said a treasury dealer in Shanghai.
After a cut in the bank reserve rate, commercial banks would have more funds available for lending.
China has already banned the use of bank funds from stock market speculation, so the impact on the markets would be less than a cut in bank deposit rates, analysts said.

"A cut in the reserve ratio wouldn't have as much an impact on people's private savings as an interest rate cut," said an analyst at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai. "The connection to the stock market is more tenuous."
But a cut in the reserve ratio would not reduce the interest rate burden of many companies that are struggling to repay loans, analysts said.
More money would be available for lending but many potential borrowers would be unable to afford the cost of funds.
"Cutting the reserve ratio and keeping interest rates high will make debt service tough," the foreign securities firm analyst said.

People's Bank officials declined to comment on the possible timing of a cut in the bank reserve ratio or interest rates, but one said the central bank would examine the market situation before making any decision.
China's listed companies are generally expected to show poor results when they make their 1997 interim reports in August, leading to a further outcry for credit easing, analysts said.
